name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
      - name: Run unit tests
        run: npm test
      - name: Build production bundle
        run: npm run build

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm ci && npm test && npm run build

  deploy:
    needs: build-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production   # configured in the repo with 2 required human reviewers
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh

#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/pre-push
echo "Running local checks before push..."
npm test && npm run lint
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Local checks failed -- push aborted. Fix issues or use --no-verify to override."
  exit 1
fi

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm test

  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh
expl: By default, jobs defined in the same workflow file run independently and in parallel unless a `needs:` relationship links them -- the engine has no idea `deploy` is supposed to depend on `test` passing just because they happen to be written in the same file. Without `needs: test`, `deploy` starts immediately when the workflow triggers, completely regardless of whether `test` ever finishes or what it reports. Adding `needs: test` makes `deploy` wait for `test` to complete, and -- critically -- the default behavior is that if a needed job fails, dependent jobs are skipped rather than run, which is exactly the gate the team intended to have all along.

expl: Steps within a single job execute sequentially, and by default a CI runner stops the job at the first step that fails rather than continuing on to the remaining steps -- this default-stop behavior is exactly what makes a pipeline a usable quality gate at the step level, the same way `needs:` does at the job level. So `checkout` and `install` run normally, `test` fails and halts the job immediately, and `build` and `deploy` are never reached at all. This is a different mechanism from the `needs:` relationship between separate jobs covered in the debugging exercise above, but it serves the identical purpose: stop forward progress the moment something is proven broken, rather than pressing on regardless.

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: docker build -t app:latest .
      - run: docker run app:latest pytest

  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

expl: The original pipeline built the image twice -- once in `test`, once in `deploy` -- both tagged with the mutable label `latest`. Even though `deploy` correctly waited for `test` to pass, it then ran its own independent `docker build`, which could pick up a newer base image layer, a slightly different dependency resolution, or any other source of drift between the two build invocations. The fix builds the image exactly once, tags it with the immutable commit SHA instead of the mutable `latest`, saves it as a workflow artifact, and has `deploy` download and reuse that exact saved image rather than rebuilding. Now the bytes that were actually tested are, byte-for-byte, the bytes that get deployed -- there is no second build step in which anything could have quietly changed.

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ { run: pytest tests/unit } ]

  integration-tests:
    needs: unit-tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ { run: pytest tests/integration } ]   # this job fails

    needs: integration-tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ { run: pytest tests/e2e } ]

    needs: e2e-tests

expl: unit-tests has no dependency, so it runs first and, per the scenario, passes. integration-tests needs unit-tests, which succeeded, so it also runs -- and this is the one that fails. e2e-tests needs integration-tests; since that dependency failed, e2e-tests is skipped rather than run, by default CI behavior. deploy needs e2e-tests, which was skipped (not merely 'not yet run') -- a skipped dependency also counts as not satisfying `needs:`, so deploy is skipped too. The net effect is that a single failure partway through the chain correctly prevents everything downstream of it, transitively, without anyone having to explicitly wire up every job to check every other job's status by hand.

expl: Hashing `feature_name:user_id` and reducing it modulo 100 produces a number that is always the same for a given user and feature, so `bucket < 10` reliably picks the same roughly-10%-sized group of users every single time it's evaluated -- that's the deterministic 'stickiness' the exercise asks for. Including `feature_name` in the hashed key (rather than hashing `user_id` alone) matters too: without it, every flag in the system would happen to light up for the exact same subset of users, which would make it impossible to tell, from user-level effects alone, which flag was responsible for what. Using `random.random()` instead would re-roll on every single call, meaning the same user could see the feature on one request and off on the next -- both a confusing user experience and something that would make any canary-style health metrics for the flag meaningless, since 'the 10% seeing the new version' wouldn't actually be a stable, comparable group over time.

import hashlib

def is_enabled(feature_name, user_id):
    key = f"{feature_name}:{user_id}".encode()
    bucket = int(hashlib.sha256(key).hexdigest(), 16) % 100
    return bucket < 10   # ~10% of users, deterministically

routing:
  - target: app-stable
    weight: 5
  - target: app-canary
    weight: 95
expl: The weights were attached to the wrong targets: as written, the unproven `app-canary` version receives 95% of live traffic while the proven `app-stable` version receives only 5% -- the exact opposite of a canary's purpose, and it means a bug in the new version would immediately affect the vast majority of users rather than a small, controlled slice of them. This is a realistic and dangerous class of bug precisely because the file is syntactically valid and the total still adds up to 100% -- nothing about it looks obviously broken unless you check which weight is attached to which named target. The fix simply swaps the two weight values so the small percentage (5%) goes to the canary being validated, and the large percentage (95%) stays on the already-trusted stable version.

# Non-idempotent: appends a line every single time this task runs
- name: Add app log path to logrotate config (BROKEN)
  ansible.builtin.shell: echo "/var/log/app/*.log" >> /etc/logrotate.d/app

# Idempotent: asserts the line exists exactly once, regardless of current content
- name: Add app log path to logrotate config (FIXED)
  ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
    path: /etc/logrotate.d/app
    line: "/var/log/app/*.log"
    create: true

- name: Set APP_ENV variable (BROKEN)
  ansible.builtin.shell: echo "APP_ENV=production" >> /etc/environment
expl: The original `shell` task has no notion of 'is this line already present' -- `echo ... >> file` unconditionally appends on every single execution, so three playbook runs leave three identical lines in `/etc/environment`, which is both wasteful and can cause real problems if something downstream parses that file expecting one value per key. `lineinfile` is a module purpose-built for exactly this assertion: it checks the file's current contents and ensures the specified line exists exactly once, adding it only if it's missing and leaving the file untouched if it's already there. This converts the task from 'a command that runs every time' into 'a state that either already holds or gets corrected to hold,' which is what makes it safe to include in a playbook that might legitimately run against the same machine dozens of times over its lifetime.

expl: `[production:children]` declares that the `production` group's membership is the union of the `web` and `db` groups' hosts -- specifically web1, web2, and db1. `cache1.example.com` belongs only to the `cache` group, which was never listed under `production:children`, so `--limit production` does not include it at all, even though it's a perfectly valid host elsewhere in the same inventory file. This is exactly the kind of targeting mistake that's easy to make in a large inventory: a new group gets added for a new service, but nobody remembers to also add it to the higher-level group that broader playbook runs target, so that service quietly never receives configuration changes intended for 'all of production.'

expl: The original shell pipeline reads the current crontab and appends a new line to it every single time the task runs, with no check for whether an equivalent entry already exists -- four runs during testing produced four identical scheduled jobs, meaning the cleanup script would have actually executed four times every night in production. The `cron` module is purpose-built to manage individual entries idempotently: it identifies a specific cron job by its `name` (stored as a comment marker in the actual crontab) and updates that one entry in place on subsequent runs rather than blindly adding a new line, converging to exactly one job with that name regardless of how many times the task executes.

exp: Run 1: the file doesn't exist yet, so the template task reports changed and deploys it; the handler fires and restarts the app. Run 2: the file already matches the template exactly, so the task reports ok, no changed occurs, and the handler does not fire -- the app is not restarted. Run 3: the manual edit means the file no longer matches the template, so the task reports changed again (overwriting the manual edit with the templated content) and the handler fires again, restarting the app.
code:
tasks:
  - name: Deploy app config
    ansible.builtin.template:
      src: app.conf.j2
      dest: /etc/app/app.conf
    notify: restart app

handlers:
  - name: restart app
    ansible.builtin.service:
      name: app
      state: restarted
expl: Each run is governed by the same rule: the template task compares the file's actual current content against what the template would render, reports `changed` only on a mismatch, and the handler fires only when notified by a task that actually reported `changed`. Run 1 has no file yet, a mismatch by definition, so it changes and restarts. Run 2 has a file that already matches (deployed by run 1, with nothing else touching it since), so it's a clean `ok` with no restart -- exactly the idempotent no-op a second identical run should produce. Run 3 has drift introduced by the manual edit; the templated content still doesn't match that edited file, so the task again reports `changed`, silently overwriting the manual edit back to the declared desired state and restarting the app to pick it up -- this is the reconciliation behavior that makes idempotent configuration management useful for correcting drift automatically, not just for safely doing nothing on unchanged machines.

DB_PASSWORD = "Sup3rS3cr3tProd2025!"

import secrets_client

    return connect(host="db.internal", user="app", password=password)

expl: The fix has two genuinely separate parts, and doing only the first without the second leaves the actual danger fully intact. First, `db_password` is removed from the plaintext vars file entirely and replaced with a runtime lookup against a secrets manager, so future commits never contain the plaintext value at all. Second -- and this is the part that's easy to skip but is the one that actually matters -- the existing production database password must be rotated to a brand-new value, because the old one is already present, in plaintext, in this repository's git history, visible to anyone who has ever had clone access. Editing the file to remove the password going forward does nothing to un-expose the value that was already committed; only generating a new credential and revoking the old one actually neutralizes the exposure.

expl: `printenv` dumps every environment variable available to that job step, and CI systems typically inject secrets (API keys, database passwords, cloud credentials) as environment variables specifically so application code can read them -- meaning this debug step printed every one of them, in plaintext, directly into build logs that are frequently readable by a much wider group of engineers than should ever see production secrets. Removing the step stops the leak going forward, but exactly like the git-history case, it does nothing to un-expose whatever secrets were already printed into historical log runs while the step existed -- those specific secret values need to be rotated, and any historical logs that captured them should be checked for retention and access, since the leak already happened the moment the pipeline ran with that step in place, not merely if someone is later found to have looked at the log.

SCENARIO A: Under deadline pressure, an engineer skips the usual staging deploy
and pushes straight to production, following an undocumented but common team
norm that 'staging is basically always green anyway.' The deploy breaks prod.

SCENARIO B: An engineer, annoyed that a required approval step slows them down,
deliberately disables it in the pipeline config so future deploys skip it
entirely, telling no one. A later deploy breaks prod because of exactly the kind
of issue the approval step existed to catch.

Month 2: 3 near-miss reports filed

1. An engineer, following the documented deploy process exactly as written, deploys

2. An engineer skips writing a test for a 'small' change because the team has an

3. An engineer, frustrated that a security scan is slow, permanently disables it

expl: Scenario 1 involves no deviation from agreed process at all -- the gap is entirely in what the process itself could catch, which is a systems question, not a personal one. Scenario 2 involves a deviation from written policy, but one that was normalized and widely shared across the team rather than an individual secretly acting alone, which points to a team-wide incentive or friction problem rather than one person's judgment. Scenario 3 is qualitatively different from both: it's a single individual's deliberate, hidden, sustained choice to disable a safeguard that everyone else believed was still protecting them, which is exactly the kind of conscious disregard of a known risk that Just Culture treats as warranting real individual accountability, distinct from the systemic response appropriate to the first two.

expl: The declining reporting trend is best explained by a hidden contradiction between the stated policy and an actual practice: even though the postmortem document itself is genuinely blameless, a separate channel (private manager notes feeding promotion discussions) means that being honestly involved in an incident still carries a real career cost -- just one that isn't written down anywhere the engineers can see or point to directly. People tend to detect this kind of contradiction eventually, whether through a leaked comment, an inconsistent promotion outcome, or simple pattern-matching over time, and once they do, they rationally revert to protecting themselves regardless of what the official document promises. This is exactly the mechanism described in the concept: culture is established by what actually happens, not by what's declared, and a single hidden channel connecting candor to consequence is enough to undo an otherwise well-designed blameless postmortem process.

def error_budget_minutes(slo_percent, window_days=30):
    total_minutes = window_days * 24 * 60
    allowed_failure_fraction = 1 - (slo_percent / 100)
    return total_minutes * allowed_failure_fraction

print(error_budget_minutes(99.95))   # 21.6 minutes over 30 days
print(error_budget_minutes(99.99))   # 4.32 minutes over 30 days

def budget_status(slo_percent, window_days, downtime_minutes_so_far):

    allowed_downtime = total_minutes * (1 - slo_percent / 100)

    return (round(remaining, 2), should_freeze)

# provision-worker.sh
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Role,Value=worker}]' \
  --count 1
expl: The original script unconditionally calls `run-instances` every time it executes, with no notion of 'does a worker already exist' -- so a CI retry, which by definition re-runs the exact same step, creates a second worker instance identical in every way except its instance ID. The fix adds an explicit existence check via `describe-instances` filtered by the same tag the script itself sets, and only creates a new instance if none is found running or pending. This is exactly the kind of hand-written idempotency logic that a declarative tool like Terraform gives you automatically for every resource type -- which is the deeper lesson: imperative scripts *can* be made idempotent, but only by manually re-deriving, for every single resource, the same diff-and-reconcile behavior that declarative tooling provides as a first-class, built-in guarantee.

  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId' --output text)

if [ -z "$EXISTING" ]; then

    --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 \
    --instance-type t3.micro \
    --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Role,Value=worker}]' \

## Disk Almost Full on Database Host (paired with alert: DiskUsageHigh)

### Symptom/Detection
Alert fires when disk usage on a database host exceeds 90%. Confirm with:
`df -h /var/lib/postgresql` -- if Use% is above 90%, this is real, not a false alarm.

### Immediate Mitigation (buys time, not a permanent fix)
Clear old WAL archive logs older than 7 days, which are safe to remove:
`find /var/lib/postgresql/wal_archive -mtime +7 -delete`
Recheck `df -h` -- this typically frees 10-15% within a minute.

### Diagnosis
If usage climbs back above 85% within an hour of clearing logs, this is not a
one-off spike -- check for a runaway query or an unvacuumed table:
`SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state != 'idle';`

### Escalation
If usage exceeds 95% at any point, or the quick mitigation doesn't hold for more
than 30 minutes, escalate immediately to #database-oncall -- do not wait for disk
to actually fill, since a full disk on this host causes a hard outage, not a
degraded one.

The fix gives the primary a finite window (5 minutes) to acknowledge, after which the page automatically escalates to a secondary responder, and finally, if that also goes unanswered, to an engineering manager as a guaranteed last resort. This closes the single point of failure the same way adding a failover replica closes one for a service -- the system as a whole no longer depends on one specific person being reachable at one specific moment for the escalation to work at all.

# CHANGELOG.md (proposed)
## 2.3.1
- Removed the deprecated `formatLegacy()` export.

# proposed command:
# git tag v2.3.1 && npm publish
expl: Removing a still-callable public function is, by definition, an incompatible change to the library's public contract -- any consumer still calling `formatLegacy()` will break immediately on upgrading, with no code change of their own. A PATCH bump (2.3.0 -> 2.3.1) promises exactly the opposite: that nothing consumer-facing changes except for a corrected bug. Worse, a consumer pinned with `~2.3.0` (patch-only upgrades) or even `^2.3.0` (minor/patch upgrades) would have their tooling automatically accept this version with no warning at all, since both ranges are built on trusting that a non-major bump won't break them. Tagging this 3.0.0 instead correctly signals 'stop and check before upgrading,' and per-semver convention, `^2.3.0`-style ranges will not automatically resolve to a 3.x version at all, giving consumers the chance to review the breaking change deliberately before opting in.

expl: `^1.4.2` is interpreted as 'anything from 1.4.2 up to, but not including, 2.0.0,' which is exactly the range of versions semver promises will remain backward compatible with 1.4.2. Among the published versions, 1.4.5 and 1.9.0 both fall within that range, and the package manager resolves to the highest matching one, 1.9.0, to get the most up-to-date compatible release. 2.0.0 sits outside the range specifically because it carries a different MAJOR number, which by definition may include incompatible changes -- accepting it automatically would defeat the entire purpose of declaring a `^` range in the first place, since the consumer would be silently exposed to changes semver never promised would be safe.

expl: The check itself is intentionally simple -- a kill switch's logic should be as close to foolproof as possible, since it's meant to be trusted during an active incident. The important design decision is where `kill_switch_cache` actually lives: it must be a store independent of the recommendation engine and whatever shared infrastructure (like a primary database under load) might be causing the slowness in the first place. If the switch's own state were stored in that same struggling system, flipping it during an incident could be exactly as slow or unreliable as the problem it's meant to solve -- a circular dependency that defeats the purpose of having a kill switch at all. A small, dedicated, highly-available key-value store with minimal dependencies of its own is the standard choice, precisely because it needs to keep working when almost everything else might not be.

-- if for some reason it's still null; old code, if rolled back to, still works

2. New application code deployed, relying entirely on `email`.
3. A bug is discovered: password reset emails are being sent to the wrong
   address for accounts with certain email formats.
4. Team considers rolling back to the previous application version.

-- Single migration, deployed together with the new application code:
ALTER TABLE subscriptions ADD COLUMN renewal_period TEXT NOT NULL;
-- New app code writes renewal_period on every insert/update.
-- Old app code (the rollback target) never sets this column at all.
expl: The original plan collapses expand and contract into a single step: the column is both introduced and immediately made mandatory in the same migration that the new code starts depending on, which means a rollback to the previous code -- which never sets this column -- would violate the `NOT NULL` constraint on every write, exactly as in the worked example in this concept. The fix separates the phases: this release only expands (adds the column nullable, with application code tolerant of it being absent), which keeps the previous code version fully rollback-safe, since nothing about the schema yet requires what old code doesn't provide. The `NOT NULL` constraint is deferred to a later, separate release, made only once the column has been reliably populated for a while and there's real confidence a rollback won't be needed -- at which point tightening the constraint is a much lower-risk, deliberate contract step rather than an accidental one bundled into the original change.

-- it, does not violate any constraint if rollback is needed here.

-- MIGRATE (later release, after this one has soaked): app code now relies on
-- renewal_period more fully, backfilled for historical rows.

-- CONTRACT (still later, after further confidence): only now --
ALTER TABLE subscriptions ALTER COLUMN renewal_period SET NOT NULL;

The only viable path is roll-forward: keep the current (buggy but at least schema-compatible) code running, and ship a specific, reviewed fix for the actual bug on top of it, accepting that reverting is off the table once a migration has destroyed information a prior version depended on.
